problem: End-to-end navigation planners (iPlanner, ViPlanner, NavDP) still depend on external localization (SLAM/VO) that needs precise camera-chassis extrinsic calibration. They process single frames or short clips, so they lack long-term history and metric-scale geometry memory, leading to drift and inconsistent planning.
motivation: Modular pipelines suffer cascading errors and latency, and on legged robots gait-induced vibration degrades odometry. A fully end-to-end policy that estimates its own state and reconstructs metric geometry from visual history could generalize across embodiments and camera placements without calibration.
key_idea: Fine-tune a long-horizon visual-geometry backbone (VGGT) with depth-injected metric scale to predict pose and metric point clouds, and condition a diffusion trajectory policy on the resulting implicit state and geometry features through task-specific queries.
insight: Auxiliary supervision on odometry, goal and point cloud materially improves planning: SR on Home goes 49.5 -> 51.3 -> 52.4 -> 57.3 as each is added, with point cloud giving the largest jump. Metric-scale injection matters: VGGT without depth prior gets 54.9 SR / 0.87 PE on Home, versus 57.3 / 0.55 with it. Multi-frame geometry backbones beat single-frame DepthAnything (49.9 SR).
method: Metric-aware geometry backbone: VGGT with DINOv2 image patch tokens fused with tokens from a lightweight ViT encoding depth maps, so scale priors enter at patch level. Alternating intra- and inter-frame attention with RoPE gives metric-aware per-frame features.
Auxiliary heads: a local point head (supervised by depth back-projected into the camera frame) and a camera pose head (camera-to-world in the last-frame chassis coordinate system).

World point prediction: local-point and pose features are concatenated, fused by a context module, and decoded to metric world points in the last chassis frame, using a sign(z)(exp|z|-1) output transform.

Chassis/camera decoupling: predicts the chassis pose (x, y, yaw) and the relative goal from pose features, with no explicit extrinsic calibration. Training data randomizes camera height and pitch for cross-embodiment robustness.

Query-based policy: state queries cross-attend pose features and geometry queries attend point features. Together with the goal embedding they pass through a transformer decoder to give a planning context Q_P, avoiding explicit pose/point-cloud hand-off.
Diffusion policy head: denoises action chunks (dx, dy, dtheta) conditioned on Q_P.
Two-stage training: stage 1 fine-tunes the backbone decoder and heads (batch 12, 24 h). Stage 2 trains the diffusion head with the decoder frozen (batch 32, 3 days).

setting.backbone: VGGT (DINOv2 ViT, fine-tuned decoder) + depth ViT encoder + query transformer + diffusion policy head
setting.training_data: InternData-N1 style simulated navigation dataset: >200k trajectories, ~10M rendered images, ~2k scenes. Robot height randomized 0.25-1.25 m, camera pitch 0-30°; A* paths smoothed with splines.
setting.action_space: Predicted trajectory / action chunks (dx, dy, dtheta) in chassis frame

numbers_note: Simulation benchmark is a self-built InternScenes test set (40 unseen scenes), not a canonical benchmark. NE/PE come from the backbone ablation table. Real-world SR values are printed as percentages with counts.
results: Without any external localization, LoGoPlanner reaches 57.3 SR / 52.4 SPL on Home and 67.1 / 63.9 on Commercial. This beats ViPlanner even with oracle localization (45.0/43.2 and 63.7/61.9), a 27.3-point Home SR gain. In real-world tests it gets 85/70/50% SR on TurtleBot/Go2/G1 versus ViPlanner's 50/45/0%.
limitations: Real-world reconstruction quality is unsatisfactory because only ~2k navigation scenes were available for training; real-world metric-scale data is still being collected.
Assumes the camera has no yaw offset relative to the chassis, and evaluation is limited to point-goal navigation in a self-built simulation set plus 20 trials per real platform.
Inference runs on a cloud RTX 4090 rather than onboard, and training is expensive (about 4 days).
